title: Rabin-Karp (Rolling Hash)
tagline: Match by comparing hashes, sliding the window in O(1) per step with a rolling hash.

intuition.analogy: Instead of comparing two long documents word-by-word, you compare their 'fingerprints' (a hash). If fingerprints differ, the documents differ. If they match, you do a quick full check to rule out the rare coincidence.
paragraphs: Rabin-Karp matches a pattern by hashing it and comparing against the hash of each window of the text. The breakthrough is the rolling hash: when the window slides one character, you update the hash in O(1) by removing the outgoing character and adding the incoming one.
Treat the string as a number in some base (e.g. 256 or 31) modulo a large prime. Sliding multiplies by the base, subtracts the leaving character's contribution, and adds the new character.

Hash collisions are possible, so on a hash match you verify the actual characters. With a good modulus, collisions are rare and the average run is linear — and the rolling-hash idea generalises to substring comparison, deduplication, and 2D matching.
intuition.keyIdea: Compare cheap rolling hashes; only do a full character check when hashes collide.

steps.title: Hash the pattern and first window
steps.detail: Compute polynomial hashes of the pattern and the text's first m characters under a base and large prime modulus.

steps.title: Roll the window
steps.detail: Slide by one: hash = (hash − leaving·base^{m−1})·base + entering, all mod p.

steps.title: Verify on match
steps.detail: When window hash == pattern hash, compare characters directly to confirm (guarding against collisions).

complexity.time: O(n + m) average, O(n·m) worst (many collisions)
complexity.timeReason: Each slide is O(1); verification is rare with a good hash.

pitfalls: Always verify on a hash match — never trust the hash alone.
Use a large prime modulus (and possibly double hashing) to avoid anti-hash adversarial inputs.
Mind modular arithmetic: keep values non-negative after subtraction.

dryRun.clickMoment: Each window's hash was derived from the previous one in O(1) — no re-hashing of all m characters. The expensive character comparison happened only once, on the true match.

approach: Hash the pattern, then roll a hash over each window of the text: dropping the leading character and adding the trailing one in O(1).
When hashes match, verify the substring to guard against collisions. Use a large prime modulus.

problems.title: Longest Duplicate Substring
problems.statement: Longest substring occurring more than once.
problems.hint: Binary search the length + rolling-hash set membership.

approach: Binary search the answer length L (duplicate-existence is monotonic). For a given L, hash every length-L window and look for a repeat.
Store seen hashes in a set; on a hash hit, verify to avoid collisions. Each check is O(n), so total O(n log n).

problems.title: Distinct Echo Substrings
problems.statement: Count substrings of the form t+t.
problems.hint: Hash substrings to compare halves in O(1).

approach: An echo substring is t+t. For every possible half-length L, slide and compare the two halves using prefix hashes in O(1).
Collect distinct echo substrings by their hash (verify on hit). Iterate L from 1; total O(n^2) with hashing.

problems.title: Longest Common Subpath
problems.statement: Longest path common to all sequences.

approach: Binary search the common-subpath length L (monotonic). For each L, hash all length-L windows of every path and intersect the hash sets.
If the intersection across all paths is non-empty, length L is feasible. Use a strong 64-bit modulus to keep collisions negligible.
